title: controversial take: "generated worlds" will never make a real game. the tech isn't the problem, the whole idea might be.
author: legendpizzasenpai
selftext:
I build with AI in games and I'm about to say something this sub might hate, but I actually want to be proven wrong.

every world model demo looks incredible for 30 seconds. an infinite generated world, a playable dream, a level that builds itself as you walk. everyone loses their mind. and then... no game ever ships from it. ever. it's been this way for a while now and I've started to think it's not a coincidence.

here's my actual take: a generated world that changes every frame is the opposite of a game. games need consistency. a door that was locked five minutes ago has to still be locked. an enemy you killed stays dead. the map has to be the same map when you walk back. "generated in real time" and "coherent enough to actually play" might be fundamentally at war with each other, and no amount of better models fixes a design contradiction.

so the demos aren't lying about the tech. the tech is genuinely getting good. they're lying about the game, because there is no game, just a vibe you can walk around in for a minute before it forgets itself.

BUT. I could be completely wrong, and that's why I'm posting here instead of just ranting. maybe the answer isn't "generate the whole world" but "generate the boring parts and pin the important state." maybe there's a genre that actually WANTS a world that never repeats.

so tell me straight, you people actually building this stuff:

* is a persistent, playable generated game genuinely possible, or is real-time generation just a fancy tech demo that'll never be a shipped game?
* if you had a live world model you could control in real time with one API call, is there a game you'd actually build with it, or would you still reach for a normal engine every time?

genuinely trying to figure out if this category is the future of games or a beautiful dead end. rip into it.

comments.author: anotherlebowski
comments.body:
You've hit the nail on the head, and it's a limitation of AI itself.  The real world is grounded in objective reality.  

Gravity exists, so if you film a video, it will necessarily obey the laws of gravity, but an AI video only has a likelihood of obeying gravity. 

Facts are objectively true, but AI only has a likelihood of stating that fact accurately.

The state of a game (door is locked) is objectively true, but AI only has a likelihood of persisting that state. 

People will counterargue that all games have bugs and humans make mistakes, so the door may mysteriously become unlocked in a human developed game, but a bug is very different from the fundamental architecture of the game not respecting state persistence.

Again, this gets back to the fundamental way AI works.  It's based on training data.  That's the anchor. The model itself will drift from the training data, like when you tell AI to keep generating the same picture over and over and it slowly morphs into an abstract, faceless blob.  Reality doesn't work that way.  The training data itself is based on facts that were arrived at by humans based on science or math or inductive reasoning.  The model is making a lot of probabilistic associations between those already existing data points, represented as words and characters and pixels, and despite the fact that it's almost magically effective, I'm a firm believer that this probabilistic model takes us out of "objective" space and into "likelihood" space, which means in your game we're not able to determine the door will persistently remain locked, as opposed to becoming unlocked, not having a keyhole at all, or turning into a cupcake.  

This is why I think the best use for AI is as a documentation and snippet generator, and the real dev needs to be driven by a person.

replies.author: TemporalBias
replies.body:
> You've hit the nail on the head, and it's a limitation of AI itself.  The real world is grounded in objective reality.

So are AI systems that are grounded in physical reality with the proper "real world" sensors.

replies.author: anotherlebowski
replies.body:
Humans work the same way in the soft sense (process data to update beliefs), but not in the hard sense (we are not feed a set of training data based exclusively on linguistic tokens, and then predict the next most likely token one at a time, and then receive feedback from another human if our predictions were useful).  

People use logic, with enforced internal consistency of reasoning in a way that AI doesn't.  That's not to say that humans are "better" or "AI" isn't useful, but there is definitely something different about AI.  You can ask an AI how to do something, then give it's answer back to it and ask if it's a good idea, and it will sometimes say "no."  These blatant self-contradictions suggest that the idea that token prediction == human logic is probably not quite right.

replies.author: TemporalBias
replies.body: AI also uses logic and reasoning.

replies.author: anotherlebowski
replies.body: Sure, in its own way.  I'm not denying the usefulness of the tools.  I use them.  My stance is its good to be aware of the limitations of AI and how it's different from a person.  It encourages me to proofread everything it writes and remain diligent about challenging mistakes, which tend to be different than the mistakes of human devs I work with.

replies.author: TemporalBias
replies.body:
Sure, and I agree that understanding limitations, proofreading, and checking for failure modes are all good practices. My disagreement is not with that conclusion, but with the technical claims you used to support it.

You described limitations of particular current AI model configurations as though they were fundamental limitations of AI itself: exclusively linguistic training, one-token prediction, inability to interact with objective reality, and a lack of logic or reasoning.

AI systems can be multimodal, embodied in robots, use sensors, tools, have state, and are capable of online learning or persistent memory. Some AI systems use autoregression, some predict multiple tokens, and others use different generation methods entirely. Sequential output from AI does not imply an absence of reasoning any more than a human speaking one word at a time does.

replies.author: ididmr2
replies.body:
AI in gaming will come from very specific and well designed use cases. It needs a well defined solid world to exist within- and the intention of what they generate will have to be equally well designed.

In AI, infinity becomes nothing- its pure average, it's vague. That's what AI tends towards a worse experience the more freedom it has to create. It's an impressionist painting of a world, which is only interesting in very specific circumstances. 

The problem I see is AI games that allowing the user to create the world - the responsibility of constraint then falls on the user to enforce continuity. This should be the responsibility of the framework.

comments.author: Low-Cook-3544
comments.body:
I do believe in AI gaming. But I also believe that it hasn't reached its "Angry Birds moment" yet. 

IE all the one-off flashy parts exist (3D model generators, 3D worlds, code engine writers), but no one has truly figured out how to put them together in a way that overdelivers (or at minimum, delivers) on the promise of AI gaming. When someone figured out dow to combine graphics and mobile design in angry birds it blew up because it became so much more than the individual components. Independent labs for world models haven't cracked this and aren't investing in it enough. I don't think it should be their job to either. They're a tool provider. But whoever does figure out this breakthrough will make history.
